embedded.caption: Stowers et al. (2017), Supplementary Video 7. Zebrafish responses to real and virtual posts.
embedded.teaching_note: Comparative interface experiment: Stowers and colleagues present real and virtual posts to zebrafish. The recording concerns computer-controlled visual structure, not a sea lion touchscreen. embedded.credit: Rouse AA, Cook PF, Large EW, Reichmuth C (2016). Beat Keeping in a Sea Lion As Coupled Oscillation: Implications for Comparative Understanding of Human Rhythm. Frontiers in Neuroscience 10:257. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnins.2016.00257
embedded.caption: Rouse et al. (2016), article-provided video: Video1.MP4. Sea-lion rhythmic responding.
embedded.teaching_note: Sea-lion comparison: Ronan’s trained rhythmic head movements were studied while the sound sequence changed in phase or tempo. The paper tested adjustment of response timing after a perturbation, rather than cursor navigation. EVE’s success tone marks a completed action; the rhythm study’s repeated sounds supply timing information during an ongoing action. A sound associated with a task can therefore have different roles depending on the preparation. The movement data support behavioral timing adjustment, while coupled oscillation is a model of those data rather than a direct neuronal recording.

embedded.caption: Portugues & Engert (2011), Movie S1. Tail movements and closed-loop gratings.
embedded.teaching_note: Comparative feedback preparation: Portugues and Engert record zebrafish tail movements and visually controlled gratings. Closed-loop presentation relates the animal’s own movement to the stimulus it receives. In EVE, visual cursor feedback instead follows directional-button input. These distinct preparations separate response production from the sensory consequence used to adjust the next action. The tail movement is not a touchscreen response.

embedded.caption: Stowers et al. (2017), Supplementary Video 13. Zebrafish portals and virtual swarms.
embedded.teaching_note: Comparative animal-controlled visual environment: zebrafish move among rendered agents and portals in Stowers and colleagues’ study. Entering a portal changes the presented virtual world. EVE changes target position while retaining the cursor-to-button relationship. Both preparations couple animal behavior to software-defined visual conditions, but their motor actions and reward arrangements differ. The fish footage is not evidence of sea-lion learning.

embedded.caption: Zebunke et al. (2018), Supplementary Video 3. Switching from waiting to the immediate reward.
embedded.teaching_note: Comparative change of choice: a pig interrupts waiting and switches to the immediately available reward in Zebunke and colleagues’ study. The change ends the opportunity for the larger delayed reward. In the EVE failure condition, an incorrect choice ends that trial’s opportunity for reward. These are different contingencies: the pig can select another reward, whereas the failed EVE trial supplies none. The shared teaching issue is how the current response changes the remaining opportunity.

late_slide_recordings.caption: Gruber et al. (2019), Video S1. Physical-object demonstrations.
late_slide_recordings.teaching_note: Gruber and colleagues record demonstrations of the functions of four physical objects to chimpanzees before a matching-to-function task. Two objects open the box and two merely contact it. The later matching phase described in the paper pairs objects by function; the recording itself concerns the demonstrations, not a complete matching trial. This is a comparison with Pack and colleagues’ physical-object identity matching in a sea lion, not footage from that older study. Matching by function differs from choosing an identical object.

late_slide_recordings.caption: Truppa et al. (2011), Video S1. Novel four-icon transfer stimuli.
late_slide_recordings.teaching_note: Truppa and colleagues identify Video S1 with novel four-icon stimuli in a relational matching transfer test after training. The capuchin chooses according to whether items within the arrays are the same or different. This is relational matching, not literal identity between the whole sample and choice images. Novel-stimulus transfer separates responding to a relation from memorization of particular displays, but the recording does not replace the study’s performance measurements or Pack and colleagues’ sea-lion transfer evidence.

late_slide_recordings.caption: Leach et al. (2016), Movie 1. Sample, delay and nonmatching choice.
late_slide_recordings.teaching_note: Leach and colleagues record two trials of a mouse in delayed nonmatching to position. After a sample response, the mouse returns to the reward tray. A delay separates the sample from the two-choice display, and selecting the other location earns reward. The sea-lion task rewards matching identity, while this mouse task rewards nonmatching location. Both require information to persist after the sample has disappeared, with distinct stimulus dimensions and choice rules. The movie is silent in its original form.
late_slide_recordings.reference: Leach Prescott T., Hayes Jane, Pride Michael, Silverman Jill L., Crawley Jacqueline N. (2016). Normal Performance of Fmr1 Mice on a Touchscreen Delayed Nonmatching to Position Working Memory Task. eNeuro 3(1):ENEURO.0143-15.2016. https://doi.org/10.1523/ENEURO.0143-15.2016

late_slide_recordings.caption: Briefer et al. (2014), Additional file 1. Retention of a learned two-step task.
late_slide_recordings.teaching_note: Briefer and colleagues record the same goat during its last learning trial and memory tests after 28 and 281 days. Pulling and lifting components of a food box restores access to the reward. This is long-term retention of a learned two-step action, not the short within-trial matching delay tested in the sea lion. The original author labels identify the retention intervals, allowing those forms of memory to remain distinct.

late_slide_recordings.caption: Truppa et al. (2011), Video S3. Transfer to sixteen-icon arrays.
late_slide_recordings.teaching_note: Truppa and colleagues identify Video S3 as a transfer test using sixteen-icon stimuli after four-icon relational matching training. The altered array size changes the appearance of the stimuli while preserving the same/different relation. This is a comparative transfer preparation. The source does not identify every filmed trial as a first trial, so the movie must not be presented as a recording of Kastak and Schusterman’s first-trial sea-lion criterion.

late_slide_recordings.caption: Castro et al. (2026), Video S1. Choices between reward quantities.
late_slide_recordings.teaching_note: Castro and colleagues record a goat solving a reversed-reward contingency: its choice determines which quantity it receives. The study separately tracks preferences for one response side. Position must therefore be distinguished from the rewarded quantity. This task concerns reversed reward and inhibitory control, rather than the harbor seals’ serial visual discrimination reversals. The film does not establish that the displayed goat has a side bias; that question requires its choices across trials.

late_slide_recordings.caption: Padrell et al. (2022), Online Resource 1. Food-maze access and ration allocation.
late_slide_recordings.teaching_note: Padrell and colleagues record the structure and use of a tool-operated food maze for chimpanzees. Before loading it, rewards were weighed and a corresponding amount was removed from the midday snack to maintain daily caloric intake. Enrichment food therefore belongs in the complete feeding record rather than being treated as an unrelated extra ration. The movie records access to rewards, not a longitudinal offered-versus-consumed measurement or proof of welfare improvement. The sea-lion outcomes on this slide remain those measured by Winship and colleagues.
